title: Chapter 55 – Level 3
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The dead woman moves first.

She does not rise. She unfolds, as a spider unfolds in a web, in a single smooth motion with no sound in it: the cage slides from her knees to the stone, her heels find the rim of the pool, and she is standing, a thin straight figure in a mended rust cloak with the red haze moving round her ankles like water. Her right arm comes up. The black chain that is wound three times round the forearm uncoils, link by link, with a dry whisper. The barbed hook at the end of it swings, once, and hangs.

"Do not move, little boy," says Mu, in her voice. "I should so much prefer not to hurt you."

Jian does not move. He is thirty paces from her. He has three needles on their threads, a cracked rib that has begun to ache again, a Seed in his belly that has been eating a fifth of everything he takes in for fourteen weeks, and a reserve that, when he reaches for it, gives him eight and a half units where an hour ago it would have given him eleven.

The garden is drinking me, he thinks. It is drinking everyone.

The red haze is thick as soup. Every breath he draws pulls a little warmth out of him, like a hand drawing water from a well. Mu has not simply taken the Orchard. He has turned it. He has reversed the flow of the great slow tide that has fed the beds for four hundred years, and it is pouring now, silently, from every leaf and root and stone, down into the red pool, and out of the pool through a thin black thread that runs from the dead woman's heart across forty miles of dark country to a lean gray man sitting in a lily garden.

Forty miles, he thinks. And a thread.

A thread can be cut.

"You are thinking very hard," says Mu, with interest. The dead head tilts. "It is one of the things I like about you. I do not often meet people who think. They flinch, and they rage, and they bargain. You count." A faint dry rustle, like paper. "What are you counting?"

"Your breaths," says Jian.

"I do not have any."

"No." He lifts his hand. "That is the problem."

The chain flies.

* * *

It is the Narrows again, and it is not.

He had thought he knew how it would go. He has watched this woman fight, once, from forty paces up a cliff, and he has the shape of her in his head: the long whipping line of the hook, the quick turn of the wrist, the twin's matching rhythm. He expects a blur.

What he gets is a machine.

There is no flicker in the motion. No hesitation, no hint of preparation, no breath. The hook comes in a perfect straight line, at exactly the height of his throat, with exactly the speed of a thrown stone, and he has time to do only one thing. He drops. The barb passes over his head with a whine and buries itself in the white wall of the terrace behind him, and the stone bursts. A spray of chips goes into the back of his neck like grapeshot.

He rolls. He gets his feet under him. He is moving, in a low zigzag, across the broken moss toward the pool's edge, with the Veil drawn tight and the three needles trailing, and behind him the chain is already coming back, in a long smooth arc that will take his legs off at the knee.

Pebble! he thinks. Pebble, where—

Cage, she says, in a small cracked whisper. The cage is on the ground. It is by the wall. It is humming.

He sees it. A black iron box, thirty paces off, on the white stone, with the bone bars glimmering in the red light. It is resting where the dead woman dropped it. It is a long way from her. It is a long way from him.

The bars are bone, he thinks. Hollow bone.

A struck hollow vessel may be shattered.

He thinks it so clearly that for a moment the whole battlefield seems to stop. He has been looking at the wrong thing. He has been looking at the dead woman, and the chain, and the thread to Mu, and he has been thinking of a fight. But there is a much smaller thing, and a much simpler one, and it is lying on the ground at his feet, and it is made of the same material as every cage the Blood Shadow has ever built.

Spirit-ape bone, thinks Jian. Etched with a Coral Gate sigil. Not a wall. A bell.

The chain hits him in the ribs.

* * *

It does not go in. He feels it flatten against something, a dull thud, a numbing blow, and for a moment he thinks the talisman has held. Then he remembers he has not put it on. It is in his sleeve. The barb has caught in the folds of his cloak, and the loop of the chain has struck him flat across the side, and the cracked rib goes.

He does not scream. He has no breath to. The world is a white flash, and a long cold roar, and when it clears, he is lying on his back in the moss, with his mouth full of blood and the red sky wheeling above him, and the dead woman is standing over him with her head tilted.

"There," says Mu, gently. "That was the cruelty I did not wish to do. I am sorry. You are a brave boy. But you are a very small one."

The hook lifts.

Jian lies with his cheek in the moss. He is looking along the ground at the black iron cage on the white stone, ten paces away. It is trembling. In its dark hollow a small pale shape has uncurled, and one round black eye is looking back at him with such a plain stunned terror that he thinks, very clearly, in the midst of everything: No.

No. Not again. Not another one.

He gathers the thread of Qi in his palm, all of it, every drop that the red garden has left him, and does not aim it at the woman. He puts his hand flat on the moss. He closes his eyes.

The empty place, says the gate Warden's old stele, in a hand that has been dead four hundred years. Every thing has one. Inside the thing. The place where the thing is not.

He sings.

* * *

It is a different note.

He has never sung it before. He has only heard it, once, from the dark under the pool: a deep, soft, round tone, the bell-voice of a great hollow, like the sigh of a very large animal in a very small cave. It was not his. It belonged to the room below. But it has been in his head ever since, humming, like a tune he cannot put down, and now, with his palm on the dying moss and his lungs full of blood, he finds he knows how it goes.

He pours the whole of his reserve into it.

The Orchard answers.

It is not a sound. It is a shiver. It goes out from his hand through the moss and the stone and the drained roots, a wave of low slow pressure, and everything that is hollow in its path begins to ring. The stalks of the dead plants hum. The glass-thin ribs of the pearl-gray terrace sing. The Wardens, in their ring, sixty paces away, hollow in the heart with a hundred years of rot, give out a long soft oooom, and, beside the white wall, the bone bars of the black iron cage shiver together on their pins like teeth in a frozen mouth.

Spirit-ape bone, thinks Jian. Etched in a hurry, with a key and a hook. A box that has been told to hold.

Let go.

The bars burst.

All twelve of them, at once. There is a sound like a flock of birds taking wing, a bright, brittle, silvery crackle, and a puff of fine white powder, and where the cage was there is nothing but a heap of black iron and a little cloud of dust. A small pale shape drops, very quickly, to the stone.

JIAN!

It is the loudest thing she has ever said. It is not a word. It is a roar, in the whole of his head, in his bones, a great bright rush of terror and joy and relief that nearly knocks the last breath out of him. Then the recoil hits.

* * *

He has not been ready for it. He thought he was.

It is not a fist, or a hammer, or a hand. It is the whole of the Orchard, closing on him like a door. The note he sent out, pure and enormous, has gone everywhere that hollow things are, and it has come back, from every Warden and every stalk and every empty root, all at once, in a single enormous blow. It strikes him in the belly. It strikes him in the chest. It strikes him, with a long ringing crash, between the eyes.

For a moment he is not anywhere.

He comes back slowly. There is a taste of iron in his mouth, and a hum in his ears, and something warm and wet running from both nostrils and one ear. He cannot feel his left hand. He cannot see out of his left eye. The whole of the red garden is a long soft blur.

Someone is standing on his chest. It is a very small someone. It weighs about as much as a loaf of bread, and it is patting his chin, in a frantic rhythm, with two tiny cold hands.

Do not die, says Pebble. Do not die. Do not, do not, do not. I will not open the door. I will not, I will not.

"I am not dying," says Jian. It comes out as a cough. "I am only... resting."

That is what dying people say!

"Is it?"

I think so!

He laughs. It hurts. It is a thin broken wheeze, with blood in it, and he has to turn his head and spit. When he looks up again, the dead woman is standing over him, quite still, with the hook lifted and her face turned toward the broken cage.

She is not moving. That is the strange thing. She is only standing there, with the chain hanging from her fist and her empty eyes on the little cloud of white dust that was the bars, and something in the line of her thin shoulders has changed. It is a very small thing. It is the stillness of a creature that has been told one thing, and has seen another.

"Ah," says Mu, in her voice. It is a long soft breath of surprise. "That was extremely clever."

"It was an accident," says Jian, from the ground.

"I do not believe in accidents. It is a vulgar word." The gentle voice is thoughtful. "A hollow bone, and a struck note. You did not learn that in a clan. That is a Garden art." A pause. "Where did you learn it?"

"From a Warden."

"Of course you did." The head tilts. "How delightful. I begin to think I have underestimated you, little boy. I begin to think I have been very foolish."

The hook comes down.

* * *

He does not roll away. He has not the strength.

He lies in the moss, with his friend on his chest and his rib broken and his Qi gone, and watches the black barb fall toward his face, slowly, as a leaf falls, and he thinks, with a clear calm that astonishes him: There is still one thing.

It is not in his hand. It is in his head. It is the thing the interface has been trying to tell him since the first night in the Orchard, in a flat white line in the corner of his eye, in words that he has not been able to read because he was always, always, too busy to look.

Level 3 prerequisites: CE 200 [195/200].

Five short.

He has been five short for fourteen weeks. He has done the sum, over and over, in the dark, in a hundred small ways. He has fabricated, and scanned, and separated; he has spent what he had and saved what he could; and at the end of it all he has stood at the foot of a door with a hand on the latch and not been able to turn it.

It is a very small number.

Everything has a cost.

Pebble is shaking against his throat. Her small cold hands have stopped patting. He feels, through the thread, a thing he has never felt from her before, a quiet, enormous, steady trust. She is not afraid any more. She has stopped. She is only looking at him, with her round black eyes, and waiting to see what he will do.

I will not open the door, she says again, very softly. I will not. But you can.

What?

The big door. The one on the plate. A pause. Mother's door. It is not a seam. It is the other kind. It was made. It wants a gardener's hand.

Pebble—

It wants five. It says five. It has been saying it for a long time. I did not tell you. I thought you would be sad.

Five what?

Five of what you did not know you had, says Pebble.

The hook is six inches from his face.

* * *

Everything stops.

It is not like the first time, in the Orchard, when the fragment sank into his chest and the roof ran with silver. That was an opening. This is a closing. It is a long, still, shining silence, like the moment at the top of a swing, and in it, in the white wide space in the corner of his eye, a single line of text comes up, very small, very plain.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Event detected: Companion bond defended at personal cost.
Hostile overwrite: broken (Hollow Echo, resonance).
Bone-lock (Coral Gate, Pool-grade): destroyed.
Companion rescued: Seamwalker (juvenile).
Reward: +5 Creation Energy.
```

+5.

He reads it. He reads it again, and the tiny hard laugh that goes through him in the white silence is so sudden, so full, so terrible, that he almost does not notice what comes after.

```
[ARK-7 — STATUS]
Creation Energy: 200 / 400.
Qi Refining stage: 8 (early).
Level 3 prerequisites: CE 200 [met]. QR8 [met].
Access: UNLOCKED.
Ascending...
```

The silence breaks.

* * *

It is not a flood. It is not a light. It is something stranger, and much quieter, and he will not be able to describe it afterward to anyone, not to his mother, not to his father, not even to himself in the long dark hours of the nights that follow.

It is as though a hand he had never noticed has been lifted from his eyes.

He sees the Orchard. Not the red haze, not the dying beds, not the black web of the blood-thread, but the thing underneath. It is a lattice. It is a structure of fine bright lines, as fine as hairs, running through everything: stone, root, moss, mist, the bones of the Wardens and the iron of the dead woman's chain. Each line carries a faint glow. Each has a color. Some are green, and some are gold. Some are pale and clear as water. And a very few, thin and black and ugly, run from the dead woman's chest in a long straight rope, up through the ceiling of the world, into the dark.

Level 3, says the interface, in a quiet, steady white line.

```
[ARK-7 — LEVEL 3: UNLOCKED]
New capabilities:
- Scan: Structure (composition, binding, weak seams).
- Separation: LIVING TISSUE and bound agents (CE cost scales).
- Fabrication: compound (multi-component, 2 stages).
- Seam-sight: passive (partial).
Note: Separation of binding agents from a host is permitted.
```

A binding agent, he thinks. From a host.

He looks at the black rope in the dead woman's chest.

* * *

He does not get up. He does not need to. He lifts his right hand, the one he can feel, and lays it flat against the air, and with the whole of the new bright clarity he reaches into the lattice, as one reaches into a bowl of water, and finds the thread.

It is not hard. That is what astonishes him afterward. It runs through the dead woman like a nail through a plank: a hair of black blood, clotted at the root, wound a thousand times round the stem of her heart. It does not want to be moved. He feels its hunger, and its patience, and the long gentle tug of a man at the other end, forty miles away, holding the line. And he thinks, with a coldness he has never allowed himself before, of Mei Ru, dying at his feet in the green dark; of a promise made over her ashes; of a pale ghost behind an empty eye, turning, in the dark, to hear a name.

Separate, he says.

```
[ARK-7 — SEPARATION]
Target: Binding agent (Blood thread, Pool-grade) in host (deceased, Drip).
Cost: 14 CE.
Confirm?
```

Yes.

The thread screams.

It is not a sound. It is a feeling, a thin shrill wire of pain that runs up his arm and into his skull and out through his teeth, and it is not his. It is Mu's. He feels the old man's startled recoil across forty miles of night, like a hand snatched from a hot pan; he feels the sudden, wild, furious effort of a very strong will trying to hold on. For one terrible instant the line goes taut between them, and he sees, down its whole bright length, a long low room with a fire at one end, and a pine table, and a thin gray man in a chair with his hand clapped to his chest and his mouth open in a silent gasp.

I see you, thinks Jian.

And the thread comes out.

* * *

It comes in a single long black coil, like a hair drawn from a drain. It writhes. It spits. It hangs in the red air for a moment, a foot above the dead woman's breast, a thin dripping serpent of old blood, and then it curls in on itself and falls to the moss, where it lies quite still, a stained gray string.

The dead woman sways.

She does not fall. Not at once. She stands in the red light with her arm half raised, and her head turns, slowly, from the boy on the ground to the black coil in the moss, and her pearly lips part. Something happens in her face. It is a little thing. It is the melting of a mask: the stiffness goes out of the cheeks, the lids drop a fraction, and in the dry, dim, lavender eyes there is, for the first time, a spark.

It is very faint. It is a candle seen through fog. But it looks.

"Where," says Mei Lian.

It is a thin, rusty, cracked little voice. It is her own.

Jian does not move. He has no strength to. He lies in the moss with Pebble in the crook of his neck, and meets the gaze of the dead woman, and says, as gently as he can: "You are in a garden. You have been dead for some time."

"I know." A long dry pause. "I remember. The knife." She lifts one hand, slowly, and touches the stitched cut under her collarbone. "It was very... small."

"Yes."

"She said she was sorry." A faint dry sound, like a laugh. "I thought that was funny."

"Mei Lian—"

"Ru?" says the dead woman.

He has known it would come. He has known it since the quarry. He draws one breath and lets it go.

"She was burned at dawn," he says. "Behind the quarry. On pine. Nobody bowed to her." He swallows. "She asked to be burned with you. I could not find you. I am sorry. I am here now."

The wan eyes are on his face. For a long moment they do not change. Then a thin pale line, a crack in glass, runs through the waxen calm of the dead woman's brow.

"Seventeen minutes," says Mei Lian, in a whisper. "I was seventeen minutes older. I was always going to go first."

"Yes."

"She did not like to be alone."

"No. She said so."

"Then you will burn me. Next to her." It is not a question. It is almost a smile. "In the place behind the quarry. I should like to see the sky."

"I will."

"And you will tell no one that I asked."

"I will not."

"Good." The head tilts back. The hands, thin and pale, go loose. "It was a very good needle," says Mei Lian, to the red ceiling, and the light goes out of her, as a lamp goes out when the oil is gone, and she folds, quite gently, onto the moss, and lies still.

* * *

It is a very long time before he gets up.

He lies there, with the garden dying round him, and listens to it. He listens to the long slow drip of the red haze settling to the ground. He listens to the thin dry sound of the black coil, withering in the moss. He listens to Pebble breathing against his throat. And somewhere, very far away, he listens to the faint, furious, wounded silence of an old man in a lily garden who has just discovered that he cannot hold a thread.

He will come now, he thinks. Himself.

It is not a fear. It is only a fact. He turns it over, once, as he turns all things over, and puts it away.

Then he rolls onto his side, and gets one knee under him, and the other, and finds that he can stand.

The Orchard is silent. It is bleeding. Under the rim of the pool, in the wall of the lock plate, a fine thread of silver is welling up through the stone, as sap rises in a cut tree, and the red haze is thinning. The beds are gray, but not dead. The Wardens are standing, one by one, in their ring, with their heads bowed and their lamps beginning, slowly, to glow.

He walks to the terrace. He climbs the three black steps. And there, in the middle of the great dull plate with its lattice of lines too fine to look at, he kneels, and lays his palm flat on the metal.

Five of what you did not know you had, Pebble said.

He looks at the lock. He looks at it with the new eyes, with the bright thin clarity of the third level, and the lines that had always been a blur rise and part and arrange themselves, like the strings of a loom.

It is not a lock, he sees. It is a hand. It is a hand of black metal with a gap between the fingers, a gap in the exact shape of a boy's palm, and the plate is waiting for something to be laid there, very gently, and turned.

He does not know what it will do. He does not know what lies under it. But he knows that a thread has been cut tonight, and a garden saved, and a friend returned, and that in a lily garden forty miles to the east an old man is sitting up in a cold chair, with his hand to his heart, and saying a name.

It will have to be tonight, he thinks. Before he comes.

He turns his hand.

The plate cracks.

It is a clean, sweet, slow crack, like the first break of ice on a river in spring. A line of white light runs through the black metal from rim to rim. The whole great disc lifts a quarter inch. And from beneath it, from the dark, there comes up a breath of cold, dry, ancient air, and a long deep sound, like a door, a great way down, that stirs in its frame, and settles, and does not open. Not yet. But it has heard him. It has, he thinks, been waiting four hundred years to be sure.

The red haze thins to nothing. In the pool, the green comes back, a shade at a time. And from the ring of Wardens, one after another, the little lamps light up.
